claims.text: Cleric uses graduated autonomy by problem type: accuracy scores per problem class determine where the agent acts independently and where it escalates.

Cleric's Verification Engine triangulates sparse environmental signals after the fact: whether the alert recurred, whether downstream services stabilized, whether metrics recovered, and whether the engineer overrode the recommendation.

Cleric's accuracy scores update with every verified outcome, making it a closed-loop system; on problem types where accuracy is proven it can handle detection, diagnosis, resolution and verification end to end.

Resolve is designed for autonomous remediation against pre-defined workflows from the start, and its verification is open-loop: workflow execution is observable but there is no system-level measurement of whether diagnoses were correct.
Traversal performs investigation and analysis only, with no remediation; it models causal structure by building a dependency graph of the system and analyzing how signals propagate through it.
Traversal's verification is open-loop: it surfaces causal hypotheses with supporting telemetry but has no automated mechanism to verify that the inferred chain matched the true root cause.
Resolve AI is cloud-hosted SaaS with an optional in-cluster Satellite that redacts sensitive data before it leaves the customer's environment.
Resolve AI access is read-only by default and write actions need human approval, though admins can set some GitHub Actions workflow tools to run automatically.
Resolve AI starts on monitor alerts, tests hypotheses in parallel against Datadog telemetry, and proposes mitigations and fix pull requests.

Traversal's platform covers Alert Intelligence, Incident RCA, Self-healing, Code Resilience and Production Support, and each diagnosis arrives with its reasoning chain: hypotheses evaluated, hypotheses ruled out, and supporting evidence.

Resolve AI states a goal of 80% autonomous resolution and executes fixes without human intervention for well-defined incident patterns under a graduated trust model; it builds a knowledge graph of code commits, infrastructure topology and incident histories.
Cleric takes a safety-first, read-only investigation stance, delivers findings in Slack with evidence links and confidence scores, and learns from engineer feedback.

Cleric's action surface is deliberately scoped: it runs defined runbook actions and read-only diagnostics but does not execute arbitrary mitigations, and the bound is meant to be enforced by the tool rather than by policy alone.
An evidence trail for an AI SRE is the auditable record of queries run, spans and log lines cited, model and prompt used, hypothesis, mitigation suggested or executed, outcome and confidence.

Datadog's Bits AI SRE, launched in Limited Availability at DASH, investigates alerts 24/7 by analyzing runbooks and telemetry, validates its own findings, and delivers a conclusion to collaboration tools before on-call responders log in; it supports HIPAA workloads and RBAC.

Datadog's Bits AI suite includes Bits Investigation for alert triage and RCA, Bits Code for generating fixes and opening PRs, and a Bits Agent Builder for custom agents; these agents see only what Datadog sees.
PagerDuty's SRE Agent triages alerts, runs diagnostics and executes runbooks as a virtual responder in the on-call roster, can suggest remediation before a human is paged, and has 700+ integrations.
Middleware OpsAI traces errors to the exact line of code via GitHub MCP and either opens a PR with a fix or auto-applies the fix for Kubernetes.
The IDC 2026 AIOps MarketScape noted New Relic's SRE Agent offers human-in-the-loop controls, approval gates and example workflows for automated rollbacks.

Auto-execution of remediation is rare and usually limited to well-understood actions like rolling back a recent deployment; evidence from real incidents suggests over-reliance on automation can double recovery times when it fails and humans are pulled in cold.
A 2026 buyer's guide describes a trust-gradient model: AI-assisted investigation, then human-approved remediation, then bounded autonomous execution.

Google's SRE framework defines L3 High Autonomy as independently detecting, deciding and acting without human approval for bounded actions in well-defined scenarios, and L4 Full Autonomy as devising multi-step action sequences, monitoring intervention impact, trying alternative mitigations and initiating rollbacks.

Google's AI Operator is a first-responder agent that runs RCA and selects a mitigation; it operates at L2 (human SRE accepts suggestions for critical operations) and L3 (autonomous execution for minor incidents).

Google routes agent mitigations through an Actuation Agent acting as a safety gateway, which runs pre-flight validations including mandatory dry-runs, justification checks that the action targets an open incident, and concurrent action checks.

Google's safety controls include distinct, strongly authenticated agent identities with on-demand least-privilege access, agent-specific rate limits and circuit breakers, interruptible actions, real-time risk evaluation (deployments, error budget, active incidents, time of day), and logging of signals, hypotheses, reasons and confidence.
